beats.narration_text: Hello. I'm Shreevarshun Saa-thee-ya-moorthy. New graduates on O P T ask which companies are hiring. Better to ask which have actually sponsored people at my level.

beats.narration_text: A record: a value from a real file or tool output. A model judgment: a value an AI produced, not yet checked. A gate: a rule that stops the run when evidence is missing.

beats.narration_text: This is my project: a command line pipeline that shows an international new graduate which companies have sponsored people at their level. When it's done, it will refuse to call a job open unless a record backs it. I built the prototype for my INFO seventy-three seventy-five Assignment 2, in early October 2026.

beats.narration_text: It will save new graduates the manual cross-checking of sponsorship history against live postings. Sponsor sites like Ellis and F1Jobs count past visa filings; mine will also check that a posting is live, and match occupation and level.

shot.visual_intent: Left: a tall stack of filing pages with a counter (past filings). Right: one posting page. A dashed cable draws between them; a liveness lamp and an occupation tag appear on the cable as 'will' parts.

beats.narration_text: In the first minute, a hiring manager for an M L or AI engineer role will open the read me, run one command on a made-up persona, Meera Krishnan, and open the report.

beats.narration_text: The report opens with its warnings. Then the funnel from my worked run: thirty thousand three hundred sixty-nine companies, a hundred fourteen matching my role keywords, sixty-four entry-eligible, and fifty senior-only.

shot.visual_intent: The report page sits left with a terracotta warning dot on its first line; then three grey funnel bars grow, narrowing: 30,369, then 114, then a split bar 64 · 50 (entry-eligible · senior-only). Widths show order, not scale.

beats.narration_text: Then a conflict row: an AI web search called an Amgen posting open, the liveness check returned H T T P four oh four, so the record won, and the role went back to be verified.

beats.narration_text: Gates are hard stops. I added rule R four: when an AI claim and a record disagree, the record wins. And R five: a human check wins a same-day tie with an AI check.

shot.visual_intent: A gate drops across the conveyor; a 'model-judgment' chip and a 'record' chip meet at it; the record chip passes and the other is set aside. A second, smaller gate lights for R5.

beats.narration_text: The evidence: the commit history, fifty-eight passing offline tests, and a break attempts log. One attempt crashed the run on a missing input file; I had it fixed, and it now halts cleanly.

shot.visual_intent: An evidence binder opens: a commit strip, a test rack whose lamps light, a log page. A terminal block prints 'Ran 58 tests — OK', then a 'HALT: input file not found' line under a check.

beats.narration_text: First will come an offline evaluation log comparing AI-sourced posting claims with liveness records. It's done when one command prints an agree and conflict table, and the tests pass in a clean environment.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it is entity resolution. In my run, HUMAN INC had thirteen eighty-two approvals, but I couldn't confirm it was HUMAN Security; its sponsored titles looked like enterprise IT.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? Mostly new learning, and a real problem for students on O P T that I wanted to answer with records, not guesses.

beats.narration_text: New to me: hard-stop gates, labelled values, and catching an AI mistake against a record. I checked the Amgen and HUMAN approval counts by hand, in my own terminal.
